title: The Console
subtitle: console.log, errors, warnings, and running JavaScript live
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: When JavaScript breaks, the page just does nothing — no feedback, no error message visible to the user. Developers need a place to see what went wrong.
whyItExists.solution: The Console is where JavaScript sends output, reports errors, and takes live input. Every error includes a file name, line number, and error type — enough to find and fix the problem.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Debugging any JavaScript behavior. Checking values at runtime. Running quick experiments without creating a file.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: console.log is for development only — remove it (or use a logging library) before deploying to production.

explainModes.beginner: The Console is your browser's way of showing you what JavaScript is doing. When you write console.log('hello'), it prints 'hello' in the Console. When JavaScript crashes, the Console shows a red error message telling you exactly which line broke and why. You can also type JavaScript directly into the Console and press Enter to run it — like a calculator for your web page.
explainModes.simple: console.log(value) — print any value. console.error(msg) — print in red. console.warn(msg) — print in yellow. console.table(array) — print as formatted table. console.group(name) / console.groupEnd() — group related messages. Errors show: error type, message, file, line number, and a stack trace. Stack trace = the chain of function calls that led to the error.
explainModes.standard: The Console API is defined by the WHATWG Console Living Standard. It is available in browsers and in Node.js. console.log can print any JavaScript value — primitives, objects, arrays, DOM nodes. Objects are interactive: click the arrow to expand and explore nested properties. The Console's JavaScript REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) evaluates expressions in the context of the current page — you have access to document, window, and all global variables.
explainModes.technical: console.time(label) / console.timeEnd(label) measure elapsed time between two points. console.profile(label) / console.profileEnd(label) start and stop the JavaScript CPU profiler. console.assert(condition, message) logs only when the condition is false — useful for invariant checking during development. console.count(label) increments a counter each time it is called — useful for counting how many times a function runs.
explainModes.deepDive: The browser's Console is sandboxed — you run code in the page's JavaScript context but cannot access the browser's internal state. Chrome DevTools allows you to change the Console's execution context (top-right dropdown) to run code inside a specific iframe or Service Worker. Stack traces show the call stack at the time of the error — in production builds, source maps translate minified names back to original names. Source maps are separate .map files that map compiled code back to your source — DevTools loads them automatically when they exist.

content.text: When JavaScript throws an error, the Console shows three key pieces of information: the error type, the error message, and a stack trace showing exactly which line caused the problem.

content.code:
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
    at getUserName (app.js:42:18)     ← line 42, column 18 in app.js
    at renderHeader (app.js:15:5)     ← called from renderHeader
    at app.js:3:1                     ← called from top of file

┌─ Error type: TypeError
├─ Message: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
└─ Translation: You tried to access .name on something that is undefined
                → the variable you used is undefined, not an object

Fix: Check that the variable is not null/undefined before accessing .name
     const name = user?.name ?? 'Unknown';

items: TypeError — wrong type (accessed property on undefined/null, called non-function)
ReferenceError — variable does not exist (typo, wrong scope, forgot to import)
SyntaxError — invalid JavaScript syntax (missing bracket, unexpected token)
RangeError — value out of valid range (array length negative, too many recursion levels)

content.text: Click the file:line link in a stack trace (e.g. app.js:42) to jump directly to that line in the Sources panel with the code highlighted.
The Console as a JavaScript REPL
You can type any JavaScript expression into the Console and press Enter to run it. This gives you live access to the page's JavaScript context.

content.code:
// Inspect the DOM
document.title                     // → 'KERNAL — The core of every coder'
document.querySelector('h1').textContent  // → 'The Three Layers of the Web'
document.querySelectorAll('p').length     // → 14

// Manipulate the page live
document.body.style.background = 'red'  // page background turns red
document.title = 'Hacked!'              // changes the tab title

// Inspect stored data
localStorage.getItem('kernal_progress')  // see your saved progress
JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('kernal_progress'))

// DevTools shortcuts
$0          // the element currently selected in Elements panel
$('h1')     // shorthand for document.querySelector('h1')
$$('p')     // shorthand for document.querySelectorAll('p')
$_          // the result of the last expression

questions.question: You see: 'Uncaught ReferenceError: userName is not defined' in the Console. What is the most likely cause?
options: The variable userName has the value undefined
The variable userName was never declared — it does not exist in scope
You need to refresh the page to load the variable
The server did not return the user's name
questions.explanation: ReferenceError means the variable does not exist at all — it was never declared with let, const, or var in the current scope. Common causes: typo in the variable name, trying to use a variable before it is declared, or forgetting to import a function. This is different from TypeError: cannot read 'x' of undefined — which means the variable EXISTS but its value is undefined.

questions.question: Which console method shows an array of objects as a formatted table?
questions.explanation: console.table(array) renders an array of objects as a visual table in the Console — perfect for comparing multiple objects at a glance. Each object becomes a row, each property becomes a column. console.log(array) shows the raw array; you have to expand it manually.

faq.q: Should I remove console.log before deploying?
faq.a: Yes, in production. console.log statements slow down your app slightly and expose debugging information that end users and malicious actors can see. Use a build tool (Vite, webpack) with a terser plugin that strips console statements automatically in production builds. Keep them during development — they are your best debugging tool.

A stack trace is the list of function calls that led to the error — most recent at the top. Reading it bottom-up shows the chain: what started the chain (the entry point) → through what intermediate functions → to the line that crashed. The first line mentioning your own code (not a library) is usually where the bug is.

examples: When a React component does not render, console.log the props inside the component — if it logs nothing, the component is not being called
When an async function returns undefined, console.log right before the return — if you see the value, you have an await missing
When you need to test a regex, type it in the Console: /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test('2026-10-05')
